summary:
Ehécatl is a global web-based agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers plan resilient crop rotations in response to shifting temperatures, water scarcity, and declining soil health.
What did we develop? We built a full-stack interactive web application (Next.js, NestJS, PostgreSQL, and FastAPI) that works for any coordinate worldwide using open, credential-free Earth observation APIs. When a farmer selects a field on the map, the system automatically ingests 10 years of historical and recent data from NASA POWER (temperature, corrected precipitation, solar irradiance, and modeled soil wetness) and MODIS (250 m NDVI vegetation vigor) to detect climate anomalies and compute real, location-specific growing windows. It also integrates a field-level IoT monitoring module (ESP32 soil moisture and ambient sensors) designed as ground-truth calibration for subsequent phases.
details:
What exactly does it do? Ehécatl is a global web-based agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers decide which crop to plant next and when to transition through 24-month crop rotation plans.

  • Field-Level Satellite Diagnosis: When a user selects any coordinate (lat/lon) on the map, the platform retrieves 10 years of historical climatology and recent NASA observations to detect active climate alerts (drought, heat stress, erratic rainfall, or vegetation stress) and calculate real, location-specific growing windows.
  • 3-Strategy Rotation Comparator: It evaluates Strategy 0 ("Keep current crop") side by side against the top 2 alternative rotation sequences (1 to 3 cycles), detailing water deficits in millimeters, required fallow or cover-crop periods, soil nutrient impacts, and risks requiring local agronomic review.
  • Farmer-Priority Simulation: Farmers adjust interactive sliders (Water, Soil Health, Income, and Risk) to dynamically recalculate and re-rank strategies based on their specific resource constraints.
  • On-Field Monitoring (IoT / ESP32): Includes a dedicated zone tab to visualize real-time local soil moisture and ambient temperature/humidity readings collected at the field edge, designed to calibrate satellite estimates in future phases.

How does it work? The system integrates three core inputs into a deterministic, fully explainable agronomic engine (no "black boxes"):

1.     Credential-Free Satellite Ingestion & Normalization: A Python microservice queries NASA POWER (AG community: mean/max/min air temperature, corrected precipitation, solar irradianc, relative humidity, and modeled surface/root-zone soil wetness alongside MODIS (MOD13Q1/MYD13Q1 via ORNL DAAC and Microsoft Planetary Computer for 250 m NDVI). It computes 10-year monthly normals, detects anomalies, and identifies viable growing windows across both hemispheres.

2.     Local Context & Versioned Agronomic Knowledge: It cross-references field context (current crop, planting history, and irrigation availability) with a traceable crop knowledge base built from FAO ECOCROP (thermal thresholds and cycle lengths), FAO-56 (ET_0/ET_c evapotranspiration and K_c crop coefficients), FAO-66 (water-deficit yield response factor K_y), SARE, and USDA NRCS-328 (botanical family compatibility, nitrogen fixation, and soil erosion cover).

3.     Weighted Scoring (0–100): Each viable sequence is scored across four pillars (Water, Soil Health, Income, and Risk) multiplied by the farmer's normalized priority weights, exposing exact agronomic reasons, NASA indicators, and confidence levels.

What benefits does it have?

·        Farmer-Friendly Translation: Converts complex Earth observation metrics (such as evapotranspiration and soil moisture anomalies) into plain-language diagnostics and color-coded status indicators designed for readability under direct sunlight, while keeping raw technical variables accessible.

·        Global Coverage Without Login Barriers: Works for any coordinate worldwide without requiring NASA Earthdata accounts or country-specific seasonal calendars.

·        Water Conservation & Soil Regeneration: Helps minimize supplemental irrigation needs, break pest and disease cycles through botanical family rotation, replenish soil nitrogen via legumes, and protect bare soil against erosion.

·        Transparent Decision Support: Supports rather than replaces farmer expertise, embedding explicit reminders to validate seed, equipment, and market feasibility with local agronomists.

What do you hope to achieve? We aim to democratize NASA Earth observation data for small- and medium-scale farmers—particularly in arid and semi-arid regions facing severe water scarcity—empowering them to adapt to climate variability without taking blind financial or agronomic risks. Looking ahead, we aim to expand hybrid calibration between satellite observations and low-cost in-field IoT nodes to improve local confidence and accelerate regenerative farming adoption.

What tools, coding lenguages, hardware, or software did you use?

·        Frontend: Next.js 16 (App Router), React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Leaflet + OpenStreetMap / Esri World Imagery (interactive mapping), and Recharts (climate time-series charts).

·        Backend & Agronomic Engine: NestJS 12, TypeScript, Prisma ORM, and PostgreSQL 16 (persistent NASA data caching and multi-user JWT/bcrypt authentication).

·        Geospatial Microservice: Python 3.12, FastAPI, httpx, rasterio, and pytest.

·        APIs & Open Datasets: NASA POWER API (community=AG), MODIS/VIIRS ORNL DAAC REST API, Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC (anonymous Terra/Aqua fallback), and agronomic datasets from FAO ECOCROP, FAO-56, FAO-66, SARE, and USDA NRCS-328.

·        Infrastructure & Testing: Docker and Docker Compose (single-command full-stack deployment), pnpm, Turborepo, Jest, and pytest.

·        IoT Hardware (Field Monitoring Module): ESP32 microcontroller equipped with a soil moisture sensor (FC28), ambient temperature/humidity sensor (DHT11), and gas sensor (MQ2).
